cards.back: 1...d5 claude: We claim the center with a pawn of our own.

front.text: What is your move after 2.c4, and what is the position called?

cards.back:
2...e6 The starting position of the Queen's Gambit. claude: We cover d5 with a pawn.

2.c4 claude: The Queen's Gambit: White attacks our d5-pawn.

front.text: What are White's 4 main moves after 2...e6, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [3.Nc3] We focus on 3.Nc3, as it is the most popular move and the one that features some variations where concrete knowledge is needed.
- [3.Nf3] is a common move, but it has very little independent value for us. We play [3.Nf3 | 3...c5].
- [3.cxd5] is possible, but we play ...c5 as fast as possible and get back to the positions of 3.Nc3 c5 4.cxd5 exd5.
- [3.e3] [3.e3 c5 4.Nc3 Nf6] is a different way to reach 3.Nc3 c5 4.e3 Nf6.

White can stop our ...c5 idea with [3.c5]? though, which is premature.

front.text: What is your move after 3.Nf3 ?

cards.back:
3...c5 You see that we play ...c5 as fast as possible.

3.Nf3 is a common move, but it has very little independent value for us.

front.text: What are White's 3 main moves after 3.Nf3 c5, and where do they lead?

cards.back:
- [4.Nc3 cxd4] is covered via 3.Nc3 c5 4.Nf3.
- [4.cxd5 exd5 5.Nc3] transposes to our Tarrasch main line chapter.
- [4.e3 Nc6 5.Nc3 Nf6] leads to the line that we discuss via 3.Nc3 c5 4.e3.

front.text: What is your move after 3.cxd5, and what comes next?

cards.back:
3...exd5 claude: We take back with the e-pawn and keep our pawn on d5.

Then ...c5 as fast as possible: [4.Nc3 c5], [4.Nf3 c5] or [4.e3 c5] will lead us back to positions we reach via 3.Nc3 c5 4.cxd5 exd5.

front.text: What is your move after 3.e3, and which line do you reach?

cards.back:
3...c5 You see that we play ...c5 as fast as possible.

3.e3 c5 4.Nc3 Nf6 is a different way to reach 3.Nc3 c5 4.e3 Nf6, covered via this move order.

front.text: How do you show that 3.c5? is premature? Play the next 3 plies.

cards.back:
- 3...b6 claude: We attack the c5-pawn at once.
- 4.b4 claude: White supports it.
- 4...a5! shows that their pawn expansion was premature.

3.c5? White stops our ...c5 idea this way.

front.text: What is your move after 3.Nc3, and which opening do you reach?

cards.back:
3...c5 And we reach the starting point of the Queen's Gambit Tarrasch. We play 3...c5, taking our claim in the center and attacking White's d-pawn, just as White attacked ours.

3.Nc3 White develops their knight and increases the pressure on the d5-pawn. It is a logical follow-up to 2.c4, which is all about pressurizing our center pawn too.

front.text: What are White's 5 main moves after 3...c5, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [4.cxd5 exd5] White's main line. It usually leads to [4.cxd5 exd5 | 5.Nf3 Nc6], covered in the chapter on the main lines. Here we examine the alternatives, particularly [4.cxd5 exd5 | 5.dxc5 d4]!, which is fun to study and often gives us a great game.
- [4.Nf3 cxd4 5.Nxd4 e5] is aggressive and leads to exciting play. We quickly expand in the center and pose serious problems.
- [4.e3] is White's cautious option, covering their central pawns. It's symmetrical but will still lead to complications once the central pawn structure changes.
- [4.dxc5] A rare move with some fun points. It has some similarities to 4.cxd5 exd5 5.dxc5, but there are differences.
- [4.Bf4]? A rare move, and mistaken.

front.text: Which 2 moves can you play after 4.dxc5 ?

cards.back:
- [4...d4] We can play 4...d4.
- [4...Bxc5 5.cxd5 Nf6 6.dxe6 Qxd1+ 7.Nxd1 Bxe6] There is also the surprising option 4...Bxc5!? 5.cxd5 Nf6!, when Black has fantastic development for a pawn.

front.text: After 4.dxc5 Bxc5!? 5.cxd5, what are the next 5 plies, and what does Black get?

cards.back:
- 5...Nf6! claude: We develop instead of taking back on d5.
- 6.dxe6 claude: White grabs a second pawn.
- 6...Qxd1+ claude: We trade queens with check.
- 7.Nxd1 claude: White takes back.
- 7...Bxe6 Black has fantastic development for a pawn.

front.text: 4.Bf4? is mistaken. What are the next 3 plies?

cards.back:
- 4...cxd4 claude: We take the d4-pawn.
- 5.Nb5 claude: White hits d4 and eyes c7, which the f4-bishop covers.
- 5...e5! refutes White's concept. The simpler [5...Bb4+] works too.

front.text: What is your move after 4.Nf3, and why not 4...dxc4 ?

cards.back:
4...cxd4 The most ambitious and challenging move. There is nothing wrong with playing [4...Nc6] or [4...Nf6], but we want to seize the chance to start an early grab of the initiative. White has many ways to go wrong in the upcoming complications.

It's less convincing to capture c4, as White has promising answers like [4...dxc4 5.d5] or [4...dxc4 5.e4].

4.Nf3 A natural move, but it gives us an attractive option to reach an active position. It is popular below master-level but almost extinct amongst stronger players. They want to avoid the following line and prefer [4.cxd5 exd5 5.Nf3], the main line.

front.text: What are White's 2 main moves after 4...cxd4, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [5.Nxd4] claude: The natural recapture, which we meet with ...e5.
- [5.Qxd4]? After [5.Qxd4 Nc6 6.Qd1 d4 7.Nb5 e5], Black is much better already.

front.text: 5.Qxd4? is a mistake. What are the next 5 plies?

cards.back:
- 5...Nc6 claude: We develop with tempo on the queen.
- 6.Qd1 claude: The queen retreats.
- 6...d4 claude: We gain space and hit the c3-knight.
- 7.Nb5 claude: The knight jumps forward.
- 7...e5 Black is much better already. We gained space and time with our pawn advances.

front.text: What is your move after 5.Nxd4, and why?

cards.back: 5...e5 Here we go! We make huge strides in the center while chasing White's knight(s) around.

front.text: What are White's 3 main moves after 5...e5, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [6.Nf3] White's most common reply. The other knight moves are no improvement.
- [6.Nb3 d4 7.Nd5 Nf6] is similar to 6.Nf3 d4 7.Nd5 Nf6.
- [6.Ndb5 a6]! 6.Ndb5 is more interesting, when 6...a6! is best.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 6.Nb3 ?

cards.back:
- 6...d4 claude: We gain space with tempo on the c3-knight.
- 7.Nd5 claude: The knight jumps to d5.
- 7...Nf6 claude: We develop and challenge the d5-knight.

6.Nb3 d4 7.Nd5 Nf6 is similar to 6.Nf3 d4 7.Nd5 Nf6.

front.text: What is your move after 6.Ndb5, and why?

cards.back:
6...a6! is best. claude: We chase the knight at once.

6.Ndb5 is more interesting than the other knight moves.

front.text: What are White's 2 moves after 6...a6!, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [7.Na3]? [7.Na3 d4] is great for Black.
- [7.Qa4]! Only [7.Qa4 Bd7 8.cxd5 Nf6] works.

front.text: 7.Na3? is a mistake. What is your move?

cards.back: 7...d4 is great for Black. claude: We gain space with tempo on the c3-knight, while White's other knight sits on the edge at a3.

front.text: After 7.Qa4!, what are the next 3 plies, and what is White's problem?

cards.back:
- 7...Bd7! claude: The b5-knight is now pinned to the queen.
- 8.cxd5 claude: White grabs a pawn.
- 8...Nf6 This is a funny position, as White has gotten into a terrible self-pin. We can continue to develop (...Bc5 and ...O-O), while White struggles to coordinate their forces.

front.text: What is your move after 6.Nf3, and why?

cards.back:
6...d4 It's funny to see that we only played pawn moves so far. :-) Our position is excellent though. We have gained a lot of central space, and our pieces can develop rapidly.

6.Nf3 White's most common reply.

front.text: What are White's 3 main moves after 6...d4, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [7.Nd5 Nf6] One of the two most common moves, when we get a good game by simple means.
- [7.Ne4]? The other common move, and even worse: [7.Ne4 f5 8.Ng3 f4 9.Ne4 Nf6] gives Black a fabulous game.
- [7.Nxe5] Wait, what?! This move is scarce but could be a shock.

front.text: Which 2 moves are good after 7.Nd5, and why?

cards.back: [7...Nf6] or [7...Nc6] catches up in development while we keep the central space advantage.

front.text: 7.Ne4? is even worse. What are the next 5 plies?

cards.back:
- 7...f5! claude: Another pawn move with tempo on the knight.
- 8.Ng3 claude: The knight retreats.
- 8...f4 claude: And we chase it again.
- 9.Ne4 claude: Back to e4.
- 9...Nf6 gives Black a fabulous game. We have a huge attack after just nine moves.

front.text: What is your move after 7.Nxe5, and why not 7...dxc3 ?

cards.back:
7...f6! Very strong! We attack both knights now, and 8.Qa4+ Nd7 9.Nxd7 Bxd7 doesn't save the piece. The variation 4.Nf3 cxd4 leads to sharp and fun positions that are full of traps for White.

White's idea is that [7...dxc3 8.Qxd8+ Kxd8 9.Nxf7+] is a huge fork. This line is unclear, as White's knight likely will be stuck in the corner. There is a better solution though.

7.Nxe5 Wait, what?! This move is scarce but could be a shock.

front.text: What is your move after 4.e3, and why this knight first?

cards.back:
4...Nf6 Playing this knight first covers the d-pawn. There is nothing wrong with [4...Nc6] though: after [4...Nc6 5.cxd5 exd5 6.dxc5 Nf6], Black will regain the pawn later. It is still much simpler to prevent this option.

4.e3 White opts for a cautious setup, the Symmetrical Variation. White is a tempo up, but the position is closed and has no serious significance.

front.text: What are White's 2 main moves after 4...Nf6, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [5.Nf3] Played most of the time.
- [5.cxd5 exd5 6.Nf3] We transpose to the chapter on the Tarrasch main lines.

front.text: What is your move after 5.Nf3 ?

cards.back:
5...Nc6 Completing the symmetry. White may play 6.cxd5 exd5 again to go for a Tarrasch main line, but they can also keep the tension in the center.

5.Nf3 Played most of the time.

front.text: What are White's 4 main moves after 5...Nc6, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [6.Bd3] A simple developing move, and far more likely than 6.a3. I suggest [6.Bd3 | 6...dxc4 7.Bxc4 a6], shooting for a queenside expansion.
- [6.Be2] The same: [6.Be2 | 6...dxc4 7.Bxc4 a6]. White takes two moves to capture c4, making these two moves rather toothless.
- [6.cxd5 exd5] White goes for a Tarrasch main line.
- [6.a3] is White's main choice at the master level if they want to deviate from the main lines. We meet it the same way: [6.a3 dxc4 7.Bxc4 a6].

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 6.Bd3 ?

cards.back:
- 6...dxc4 I suggest taking on c4.
- 7.Bxc4 White takes two moves to capture c4, making 6.Bd3 rather toothless.
- 7...a6 shooting for a queenside expansion.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 6.Be2 ?

cards.back:
- 6...dxc4 claude: The same as against 6.Bd3.
- 7.Bxc4 White takes two moves to capture c4, making 6.Be2 rather toothless.
- 7...a6 shooting for a queenside expansion.

front.text: After 6.a3, what is your move, and why is 6...Bd6?! dubious?

cards.back:
6...dxc4 Simple and good. White has the extra move a3, compared to 6.Bd3 or 6.Be2. A closer look shows that it does not have a serious impact, so we can deal with White's bishop moves and 6.a3 similarly.

After [6...Bd6 7.dxc5 Bxc5 8.b4], White plays the same queenside expansion we employ. It is a sophisticated idea, but it is still rather slow.

6.a3 White's main choice at the master level if they want to deviate from the main lines. You are far more likely to encounter 6.Be2 or 6.Bd3, when we gain a tempo. If we prove to be in good shape after 6.a3 dxc4, the overall concept is sound.

front.text: What is your move after 7.Bxc4, and what is the point?

cards.back: 7...a6 This is the real point of the capture. We want to play ...b5 next and clear the excellent square b7 for our bishop.

front.text: What are White's 2 main moves after 7...a6, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [8.O-O b5] claude: White castles, and we go on with our plan.
- [8.a4] The odd move 8.a4 would stop our idea, but [8.a4 | 8...b6] would still be a good preparation for the bishop development.

front.text: What is your move after 8.O-O, and what is your plan?

cards.back: 8...b5 According to plan. White has various bishop moves, but we don't need to examine this position any deeper. We'll play ...Bb7 next and then complete our kingside development with ...Be7 or ...Bd6, followed by ...O-O. We have gained space on the queenside, and all our pieces have obtained active posts.

front.text: What is your move after 8.a4, and why is White's move welcome?

cards.back:
8...b6 would still be a good preparation for the bishop development.

8.a4 The odd move would stop our idea. White's a4-move weakens their queenside (b4-square), which is welcomed.

front.text: What is your move after 4.cxd5 ?

cards.back:
4...exd5 claude: We take back with the e-pawn and keep our pawn on d5.

4.cxd5 White's main line against our opening is 4.cxd5 exd5 5.Nf3 Nc6, when White has a choice between various tries.

front.text: What is your move after 5.Nf3, and why not 5...Nf6 ?

cards.back:
5...Nc6 We have two good moves here, 5...Nc6 and 5...Nf6. I suggest the former, as I want to avoid [5...Nf6 6.Bg5], when our knight is pinned. This is not the end of the world, but playing 5...Nc6 first avoids the issue.

5.Nf3 This position is the starting point of White's main attempts to fight our opening. The most consequential decision happens on the following move, when White needs to decide about their development concept.

front.text: What are White's 5 main moves after 5...Nc6, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [6.dxc5 d4] The one direct try, when 6...d4 leads to a tactical sequence. We have seen other versions of this idea in the first chapter about the Queen's Gambit Tarrasch.
- [6.e3] White prepares kingside development, but White's c1-bishop does not look too happy about this decision.
- [6.g3] The main move at the master level, but infrequently seen below that.
- [6.Bg5] The best reply involves a possible pawn sacrifice that is not obvious.
- [6.Bf4 Nf6 7.e3] is the likely continuation, when we can choose between simple development or the more ambitious 7...c4!

front.text: After 5...Nc6, which pawn structure do you regularly get, and what is its upside?

cards.back: We will regularly play with an Isolated Queen's Pawn in all these lines, as trading c5 vs. d4 is very common. Our d-pawn is a liability, but our position has a huge upside: we can easily develop our pieces to active squares. Our knights will be on the most active squares, c6 and f6, and our bishops have good prospects, too.

front.text: What is your move after 6.dxc5, and why not 6...Bxc5 ?

cards.back:
6...d4 We answer the capture as we do in other cases: advance the d-pawn.

We can't play [6...Bxc5 7.Qxd5].

6.dxc5 White captures our pawn and starts complications.

front.text: What are White's 2 main moves after 6...d4, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [7.Na4 Bxc5]! This is how we regain our pawn.
- [7.Ne4] We can choose between [7.Ne4 Bxc5 8.Nxc5 Qa5+] to transpose to the 7.Na4 variation, or [7.Ne4 Qd5]!?, when we also regain the pawn.

front.text: What are the next 5 plies following 7.Na4 ?

cards.back:
- 7...Bxc5! This is how we regain our pawn.
- 8.Nxc5 claude: White takes the bishop.
- 8...Qa5+ We regain our piece and restore material equality.
- 9.Bd2 claude: White blocks the check.
- 9...Qxc5 White has gained the bishop pair, but we have good central control and can develop our pieces easily.

It's crucial to not confuse this position with [5.dxc5 d4 6.Na4 b5], when only 6...b5! is good and 6...Bxc5? is a mistake.

front.text: After 7.Na4, why does 7...b5? not work?

cards.back: Here [7...b5]? does not work, as [7...b5 8.cxb6 axb6 9.e3] prepares the move Bb5, which is extremely annoying, as Black's knight is undefended. A key line is the tragic [7...b5 8.cxb6 axb6 9.e3 Bb4+ 10.Bd2 Bxd2+ 11.Qxd2 Rxa4 12.Bb5], when White wins!

front.text: What is your move after 6.e3, and what is your development plan?

cards.back:
6...Nf6 The natural, active square for our knight. The further development strategy is simple: we'll play ...Bd6 and ...O-O, then think about what to do with our c8-bishop.

6.e3 White prepares kingside development, but White's c1-bishop does not look too happy about this decision. This is one reason why stronger players often choose [6.g3], keeping the option to develop the c1-bishop actively.

front.text: After 6.e3 Nf6, why is this structure important, and how else can it arise?

cards.back:
After 6.e3, we have reached an important structure, as it may arise from various move orders. Our standard formation is ...d5, ...e6 and ...c5, and whenever White trades on d5 and plays e3, we reach the same pawn formation. This can happen via orders like:

- [4.e3 Nf6 5.Nf3 Nc6 6.cxd5 exd5]
- [1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 e6 3.e3 c5 4.cxd5 exd5 5.d4 Nc6 6.Nc3 Nf6], something entirely different, when the same position arises.

front.text: What are White's 2 main moves after 6...Nf6, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [7.Bb5 Bd6] claude: White pins our knight, and we develop our bishop to its most active square.
- [7.dxc5 Bxc5] You sometimes meet 7.dxc5 Bxc5, which is welcomed. The early capture gifts us a tempo.

front.text: What is your move after 7.Bb5, and why this square for the bishop?

cards.back:
7...Bd6 In the e3-setups it's best to develop the bishop to d6, the most active square. We covered e5 and pointed the bishop towards the kingside.

This is the difference to the [6.g3] system when we should play ...Be7, as White still has Bg5 to pin our knight. After White has locked in the bishop with e3, the more active move ...Bd6 is possible.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 8.O-O ?

cards.back:
- 8...O-O Very natural moves by both sides.
- 9.dxc5 Now, I want to look at the capture on c5, leading to the most common pawn structure, the IQP.
- 9...Bxc5 And we have reached the IQP pawn structure. Our pawn is isolated, but we easily develop our pieces to active squares. For a further discussion about the following play, please refer to the model game Sunye Neto-Kasparov.

front.text: What is your move after 7.dxc5, and why is the capture welcome?

cards.back: 7...Bxc5 We'll see that White often goes for the capture after we have played ...Bd6 first, so we need two moves to arrive on c5. The early capture gifts us a tempo.

front.text: What is your move after 6.g3 ?

cards.back:
6...Nf6 The most natural move ever.

6.g3 This move is White's main try at the master level. White opts for the kingside fianchetto, which has multiple ideas. A key point is pointing the bishop towards the d5-pawn, White's prime target. At the same time, White remains flexible regarding the c1-bishop. Compared to [6.e3], the bishop may still be used on g5, for example.

front.text: What is your move after 7.Bg2, and why not 7...Bd6 ?

cards.back:
7...Be7 I suggest this simple move to prepare castling.

Why choose e7 and not d6, by the way? The problem is [7...Bd6 8.Bg5], when the pin is extremely annoying. It's also instructive to realize that d6 is not a more 'active' square, as White's kingside fianchetto blunts Black's bishop. This is a difference to the [6.e3] line when we should play ...Bd6!

front.text: What is the good alternative to 7...Be7, and why play 7...Be7 anyway?

cards.back:
Black has a good alternative here: [7...cxd4 8.Nxd4 Bc5] leads to interesting complications and could be a welcome later addition to your repertoire.

I prefer 7...Be7 because the resulting positions can easily occur via different move orders. One example is [1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 e6 3.g3 c5 4.Bg2 Nf6 5.O-O Nc6 6.d4 Be7 7.cxd5 exd5 8.Nc3 O-O], when we transpose. Playing with ...Be7 is a universal solution.

front.text: What is your move after 8.O-O ?

cards.back: 8...O-O Now we have reached an important parting of the ways.

front.text: What are White's 2 main moves after 8...O-O, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [9.dxc5 Bxc5] Taking our c5-pawn leads to the IQP structure. As usual, our slightly weaker pawn structure is compensated by our piece activity.
- [9.Bg5] is the most popular amongst the 'keep the central tension' moves. Now, we have an interesting choice between two entirely different concepts.

front.text: What is your move after 9.dxc5, and what is your plan?

cards.back: 9...Bxc5 leads to the IQP structure. It's easy to find good squares for our forces, like ...Bg4 and rooks to e8 and c8 next.

front.text: What is your move after 10.Bg5, and why?

cards.back: 10...d4! An important idea: we advance the pawn to gain space. After 11.Ne4 Be7 12.Nxf6+ Bxf6 13.Bxf6 Qxf6 chances are equal. We have a nice space advantage and can try to put pressure on White's e-pawn. Our d-pawn is isolated, but White can't easily increase the pressure and win it.

front.text: Which 2 moves can you play after 9.Bg5, and how do they differ?

cards.back:
- [9...cxd4 10.Nxd4 h6 11.Be3 Bg4] We reach our usual IQP position. Our pieces are active, but White has the d5-pawn, which has an obvious target. This line is best if you prefer a more open position and active pieces.
- [9...c4 10.Ne5 Be6 11.Nxc6 bxc6] A good alternative, which leads to a more closed position. We gain space on the queenside and want to play on this side of the board. In this common continuation, White has created a doubled pawn, we get the half-open b-file and a later ...c6-c5 to activate our position.

front.text: What is your move after 6.Bg5, and why not 6...Nf6 ?

cards.back:
6...Be7 This looks best. We can't play [6...Nf6 7.Bxf6], when we either drop a pawn or need to spoil our structure by taking with the pawn.

A good alternative is [6...f6]!?, but this move is tricky to handle, as our kingside is weakened and our development gets far more complicated.

6.Bg5 We will check this move because the best reply involves a possible pawn sacrifice that is not obvious. Furthermore, the alternatives can turn out to be tricky to play.

front.text: What is your move after 7.Bxe7, and why not 7...Qxe7 ?

cards.back:
7...Ngxe7 We can't take with the queen, as it would blunder d5: [7...Qxe7 8.Nxd5].

Now, we need to study what happens if White captures c5. White can play a less greedy move, but these are easy to handle.

front.text: What are White's 2 main moves after 7...Ngxe7, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [8.dxc5 d4]! White grabs the pawn. Our usual reply to this pawn capture works well here.
- [8.e3 c4]! A less greedy move, when a good choice is 8...c4!, gaining queenside space.

front.text: What is your move after 8.dxc5, and why not 8...Qa5 ?

cards.back:
8...d4! Here we go! Our usual reply to this pawn capture works well here.

[8...Qa5] is a way to regain the material, but we have a much better move.

8.dxc5 White grabs the pawn.

front.text: What are White's 2 main moves after 8...d4!, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [9.Ne4 O-O] White's best reply.
- [9.Nb5]?? [9.Nb5 Qa5+] is a common tactic that we see frequently in this chapter.

front.text: What is your move after 9.Ne4, and what is your plan?

cards.back:
9...O-O The important concept to understand is that there is no concrete tactic to regain the pawn. We want to develop with ...Bf5 and often ...Qd5, when White will have difficulty holding the pawn in the long run. They can't easily develop due to our strong d-pawn.

Two sample lines to illustrate matters are [10.g3 Qd5 11.Qb1 Bf5] or [10.e3 Bg4 11.Be2 Qd5], when we'll ultimately win the c5-pawn back with a good position.

front.text: 9.Nb5?? is a blunder. What is your move?

cards.back: 9...Qa5+ is a common tactic that we see frequently in this chapter. claude: The check also hits the b5-knight.

front.text: What is your move after 8.e3, and what is your plan?

cards.back: 8...c4! gaining queenside space and preparing a later attack on this side of the board. White can easily drift into a passive position, while we have the easy plan ...b5-b4 to follow.

front.text: What is your move after 6.Bf4 ?

cards.back: 6...Nf6 claude: We develop the knight to its natural square. 7.e3 is the likely continuation.

front.text: Which 2 moves can you choose between after 6.Bf4 Nf6 7.e3, and what is the idea of the ambitious one?

cards.back:
- [7...Be7] Simple development.
- [7...c4]! The more ambitious move, to reach a different structure. Our idea is putting some pressure on c3, with ...Bb4, ...Qa5 and ...Ne4 ideas. This idea is logical, as White's bishop on f4 does not help to fight the pins along the e5-e1 diagonal.
